prize_parts.citation: For establishing, through designed and time-resolved experiments, the distance and driving-force dependence of long-range electron tunnelling through proteins
For the invention of base editors that convert one DNA base to another without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: My first-ranked line, long-range electron transfer through proteins (B027), is the experimental demonstration that biological electron transfer obeys physical rules: tunnelling decays with distance and depends on driving force and reorganization energy, tested in ruthenium-modified proteins with time-resolved kinetics. That is the physical foundation under respiratory chains and photosynthesis, which is why I weight it so heavily. The attribution is also unusually clean for this committee, since Gray and Winkler are a long-standing pair and a two-person credit leaves one slot open. The slot would go to the most strongly supported single-inventor case on the table, base editing (B008). It is a defined chemical transformation (deaminase chemistry on DNA, directed evolution of the enzyme) with a clear originator in Liu, rapid independent reproduction and early clinical use. Liu alone also avoids the Komor/Gaudelli and Nishida/Kondo allocation questions that would cost us a slot we do not have. Two clearly separated achievements, both with sharply delimited credit, make a coherent chemistry prize about how chemical mechanism is understood and how it is then engineered.
statement.case_against: B027 got only my own first-place vote in the openings and none from the other seven members. Its main weakness is that it is old and the committee may see it as established background; Marcus theory was honoured in 1992 and the surrounding field has many contributors beyond Gray and Winkler, so the 'one attributable discovery' test could be failed. Base editing follows the 2020 CRISPR prize, and the clinical record is still short, so there is a real maturity and overlap question. A pairing of a retrospective mechanistic prize with a recent engineering prize also looks like two unrelated halves and I do not claim it is the likeliest outcome. Finally, B009 has the largest Borda total and the evidence for degraders as a new modality is strong; my hesitation is purely about clinical proof and that Handa/Ito and Crews/Deshaies/Ciulli are separate strands that do not fit three names cleanly.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks PROTACs and molecular glues first as a genuinely new pharmacological modality with real consequences, led by Crews, Deshaies and Handa, and treats base editing with Liu alone as a fair configuration.
responses.response: I agree with Johan on Liu alone for base editing, and I take his 'real consequences' argument seriously. On PROTACs I differ on timing and attribution: no degrader is approved, and the PROTAC concept (Crews, Deshaies) and the cereblon/thalidomide mechanism (Handa) are two strands with a different logic, so the citation would have to cover both. I would want the expert report to tell us whether the clinical record has reached the point where we are rewarding a validated principle rather than a promising one. I keep it as my first alternative rather than my preferred choice.

responses.point: Chabes puts base editing first as a clear deaminase mechanism directed to a single nucleotide, with Liu, Komor and Gaudelli as a clean trio, and ranks reversible-terminator sequencing second.
responses.response: The mechanistic argument for B008 is persuasive and I accept it. Where I disagree is the trio: Komor and Gaudelli were the lead authors, but the Liu laboratory conceived and directed both editors, and the independent Nishida/Kondo deaminase fusion complicates a three-name credit. Naming Liu alone is more defensible on priority, and it frees a slot for a second achievement. If the committee insists on the trio, I would need to see the contribution records in the expert report before agreeing.

responses.point: Aili ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first, arguing that they made nucleic-acid drugs deliverable and are overdue after the mRNA Medicine prize, but acknowledges that attribution is spread over Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer.
responses.response: The impact is not in doubt, and I share Daniel's concern about whether the work is chemistry or formulation. My objection is procedural: six credited names for three slots, priority disputes and patents, and the distinct lipidoid line of Anderson and Langer mean the discovery is a line of work rather than a single attributable advance. I would only support it if the expert report resolves who made the decisive ionizable-lipid step, which is why I keep B016 as an alternative but not a preferred part.

responses.point: Sparr ranks phase separation first as a physical-chemical concept of cellular organization and lipid nanoparticles second, stressing thermodynamics and phase behaviour.
responses.response: I find Emma's physical-chemistry framing attractive and ranked B003 seventh for that reason. My reservation is maturity: the physiological relevance of condensates in cells, as opposed to in vitro droplets, is still contested, and overexpression artefacts remain a concern. A Chemistry prize should rest on a mechanism that has been independently confirmed in vivo, so I would not support it this year, though I would want to hear whether Emma sees the in vivo evidence as already adequate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat protein electron tunnelling as a discovery still open to recognition, given the 1992 prize for electron-transfer theory.
How to divide credit for electron-transfer experiments between Gray and Winkler and other experimental groups.
Whether the expert reports establish that Liu alone, rather than Liu with Komor and Gaudelli, is the defensible credit for base editing.
Whether PROTAC clinical evidence has matured enough, and whether degraders and molecular glues can be written as one citation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I note that B027 is close to my own research field of electron and proton transfer in respiratory enzymes, so I have tried to discount possible bias towards it. I am a Stockholm University colleague of Xiaodong Zou, but none of the shortlisted candidates is from Stockholm University to my knowledge.
